<reflection>
The first experiment provided kinetic data that fits many of the 20 candidate mechanisms with very similar negative log-likelihood (NLL) values, indicating poor discrimination. The top mechanisms (M6, M8, M7, M3, M2, M1, M10, etc.) have NLLs within a narrow range (approximately -22.9 to -22.7), while M4 and M5 are significantly worse (NLL ~ -18 and -16). The aim of obtaining an initial kinetic profile was achieved, but the data did not strongly differentiate among most mechanisms. Therefore, a new experiment is needed to perturb the system in a way that reveals differences across the entire set of plausible mechanisms.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
Increasing the catalyst concentration by an order of magnitude (from 0.01 M to 0.1 M) while keeping substrate at 1.0 M will amplify nonlinear effects arising from catalyst-catalyst interactions or higher-order dependencies. Mechanisms involving dimerization (M2, M3) will exhibit different effective rate laws because the equilibrium between monomer and dimer shifts with catalyst concentration. Mechanisms with catalyst activation (M6, M8) may show altered kinetics if activation is concentration-dependent. Inactivation mechanisms that are second-order in catalyst (e.g., M13, M18, M19) could display faster decay of activity. Conversely, simple Michaelis-Menten-type mechanisms (M1) should scale linearly with catalyst. This condition avoids extreme saturation (catalyst is still only 10% of substrate) and should yield a measurable time course that is sensitive to these differences. By comparing kinetic profiles at low and high catalyst concentrations, we can distinguish between linear and nonlinear catalyst dependencies across many mechanisms simultaneously.
</hypothesis>
